lead.text: Low-severity log-injection candidate: the JAX-RS doPost handlers of ArrayResource, ObjectResource and StructureResource in the demos/rest module take the raw HTTP POST body (a JsonArray/JsonObject/JsonStructure bound to the method parameter 'structure', fully attacker-controlled) and write it straight to the server's standard-output log via System.out.println(structure) with no sanitization, escaping, or rate limiting — the single call inside each doPost's CONTAINS_CALL set is that println. This is CWE-117 (log injection/forging): an attacker can embed newlines/ANSI escape sequences/fake log lines in the JSON string values of the POST body and have them written verbatim into application logs. This is a demo app and the sink is 'log', not one of the primary code_exec/sql/redirect categories, so impact is minor, but it is a real, grounded attacker-input-to-sink flow worth noting.

reason: The attacker-controlled-data-to-sink flow is real (verified in source and graph), but the specific CWE-117 mechanism claimed — "attacker can embed newlines/ANSI escape sequences... and have them written verbatim into application logs" — does not hold against this codebase, because `System.out.println(structure)` prints the result of `JsonArray/JsonObject/JsonStructure.toString()`, which is NOT a raw pass-through of the attacker's bytes. It re-serializes the parsed value through Parsson's own JSON generator (JsonWriterImpl -> JsonGeneratorImpl), whose `writeEscapedString()` unconditionally escapes every control character before it can reach stdout: quote/backslash get `\"`/`\\`, backspace/formfeed/newline/CR/tab become the two-character escapes `\b \f \n \r \t`, and every other char below 0x20 (including ESC/0x1B, the byte ANSI sequences start with) becomes a six-character `\u00XX` escape (JsonGeneratorImpl.java lines 541-591). This escaping is applied uniformly to both object member names (`writeStartObject(String name)` -> `writeEscapedString(name)`, line 149) and string values (`write(JsonValue)` -> `write(String)` -> `writeEscapedString(value)`, lines 262-263 and 357-360), and `JsonWriterImpl.writeObject/writeArray` route every member/element through exactly this generator (JsonWriterImpl.java lines 60-101) regardless of whether the JsonValue tree came from a builder or from parsing the POST body. Consequently a raw `\n`, `\r`, or ESC byte placed in a JSON string value of the attacker's POST body can never appear as a raw byte in the printed output — it always comes out as the literal two/six-character escape text on a single `println` line. That defeats the classic log-forging ("fake log lines") and ANSI-terminal-escape-injection techniques the lead describes as the impact. The underlying code pattern (unsanitized attacker body to `System.out.println`) is confirmed to exist, but the concrete exploit mechanism alleged is factually wrong given Parsson's own JSON serializer, so this is not a valid CWE-117 finding as stated.
evidence: Source confirmed at demos/rest/.../ArrayResource.java:42, ObjectResource.java:53, StructureResource.java:52 — all `System.out.println(structure)` on the JAX-RS @Consumes POST-body parameter. Graph query confirms all three doPost methods are :EntryPoint handlers with exposure='reachable' and the three println CpgCall nodes have reachable_from_entry=true. However, impl/src/main/java/org/eclipse/parsson/JsonGeneratorImpl.java:541-591 (writeEscapedString) shows every control character (incl. \n, \r, \u001b) is escaped to its textual JSON-escape form before being written, and JsonWriterImpl.java:60-132 shows this generator is invoked for every key/value of any JsonObject/JsonArray being serialized via toString(), which is what println(structure) actually calls.

reason:
I independently re-ran the analyst's Dependency query and confirmed the raw graph data is accurate (11 rows, exact names/versions match). However, reading the real source (as required, since the graph "lies by omission") shows the lead's central premise — that several versions are "unresolved" and therefore need manual follow-up — is false, because the Maven property placeholders are trivially resolvable from the parent POM that is sitting right there in the repo:

- /pom.xml (root) <properties> block defines: jakarta.annotation-api.version=2.1.1, jakarta.json-api.version=2.1.2, jakarta.xml.bind-api.version=4.0.0, jakarta.ws.rs-api.version=3.1.0. These are current, unremarkable Jakarta EE 10/11-era API versions — nothing suggests a known-vulnerability match, and no CVE evidence was found for any of them.
- The "${project.version}" placeholders on jakarta.json, parsson, and parsson-media resolve to this project's OWN version (1.1.3-SNAPSHOT) — confirmed by reading bundles/jakarta.json/pom.xml and rest/pom.xml, both groupId org.eclipse.parsson. These 3 of the analyst's "11 third-party components" are not third-party dependencies at all; they're this multi-module repo's own sibling artifacts, mis-captured by the extractor because it doesn't distinguish internal reactor references from external deps.
- hamcrest-core (1.3) and junit (4.13.2) are declared with explicit <scope>test</scope> (root pom.xml lines 429-434; impl/pom.xml lines 99-104) — test-only, never shipped in production artifacts. junit 4.13.2 also post-dates the fix for the one notable JUnit4 CVE (CVE-2020-15250, fixed in 4.13.1).
- jakarta.servlet-api (5.0.0) and jaxb-impl/com.sun.xml.bind (3.0.1) only appear inside the "all" profile's dependencyManagement, explicitly commented "dependencies used by demo projects only" (root pom.xml lines 444-464) — not part of the core parsson/impl/rest production libraries that constitute this scan's actual shipped code.
- I independently re-ran exploit_search for jaxb-impl, servlet-api, junit/hamcrest, Parsson, and JAXB-XXE and got the same "exploit corpus unavailable: not indexed" result the analyst reported — so no CVE could be corroborated from either session, consistent with the analyst's own caveat.

Net effect: every placeholder the analyst flagged as "could not be verified here" I resolved directly from source in minutes, and all resolve to modern, non-suspicious versions; the genuinely old components (hamcrest/junit) are test-scope only; the other old-ish component (jaxb-impl) plus servlet-api are demo-only, not production. No concrete known-vulnerability was identified for any of the 11 entries, and the "11 third-party components" framing itself overcounts by including 3 self-referential internal modules. This does not stand up as an actionable CWE-1104/CWE-937 finding — it's an SCA query artifact, not a verified vulnerable-component issue.
